text.p: American sprinter Gwen Torrence, no stranger to controversy during her highly successful career, was embroiled in more trouble on Thursday for pulling out of the Nikaia Grand Prix "for no good reason".

Torrence, seen shopping among the tourists along the bustling Rue de France in Nice on Tuesday, incurred the wrath of meeting promoter Robert Bertojo for withdrawing from the 200 metres because of what he called "vague personal problems".
An angry Bertojo added: "She could not say what those problems were and was extremely evasive.

"She is one of the stars of the sport, but she does not have the attitude of a responsible professional. She would not say why she did not want to run, just that she had decided to go back to the United States."
Torrence, scheduled to defend her world 100 metres title in Athens next month, was due to meet her old rival Merlene Ottey of Jamaica in the race on Wednesday night.
Torrence made no public comment, unlike in the past when her outspoken views about rivals have landed her in trouble with authority.
In her absence, Ottey, now 37 but running as well as ever, won the race in 22.47 seconds, the third fastest time of the year, and said she was looking forward to defending her 200 crown in Athens.
She was crowned world champion in Gothenburg two years ago after Torrence, who actually won the race, was disqualified for stepping outside her lane.
Torrence was not the only big name to withdraw from the meeting, the last grand prix before the world championships.

Missing were Sergei Bubka (pole vault), Ivan Pedroso (long jump), Kelly Holmes (800) and Frenchman Stephane Diagana, the European record holder over the 400 hurdles. Diagana said he damaged his sciatic nerve competing in Stuttgart at the weekend, but after missing the Olympics last year through injury, was determined to be fit for Athens.

While the meeting failed to live up to much of its pre- publicity which focused on two world record attempts and "200 champions", it still produced some high quality athletics and there were year's best performances in four events.
Fernanda Ribeiro of Portugal, Olympic 10,000 champion, ran the year's fastest women's 3,000 in 8 minutes 37.14 seconds. Her compatriot Carla Sacramento clocking a 1997 fastest mile of 4:25.00.
Kenya's Laban Rotich clocked the year's fastest 1,000 metres of 2:14.63, leading home a fast-finishing pack of five who all went under the year's previous best of 2:17.20.
The other outstanding performance was by Russian Maksim Tarasov, the Barcelona Olympic champion, who became only the fifth man in pole vault history to clear 6.0 metres.

He joined the elite band of Bubka (6.15), Okkert Brits (6.03), Radion Gataullin (6.02) and Igor Trandenkov (6.01) in the exclusive club with his winning leap of exactly 6.0, the best in the world this year.
Two world record attempts ended in failure despite almost perfect, still conditions under the Meditteranean moon.
Moroccan Hicham El Guerrouj failed by almost three seconds to break Noureddine Morceli's 1,500 metres record of 3:27.37 when he clocked 3:30.32.
An hour later, Morceli failed in an attempt to break his own four-year-old world mile record of 3:44.39, registering 3:48.64.
